source_document: Simply Psychology: ADHD and Working Memory (Apr 4, 2026); Marla Cummins: How This Weekly Habit Helps ADHD Adults Follow Through (updated Sep 29, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner sources, no studies tested the tip itself. The Simply Psychology page is labelled an AI-assisted draft with editorial spot review, and its studies are cited second-hand and not verified here.
text:
Recognize it when: you were told something or had a thought, meant to do it later, and it was gone within minutes.
Technique: capture it in one trusted place at once, instead of trusting your head to hold it.
How: 1. Pick one capture place you always have with you (one notes app or one small notebook).
2. Write it the moment it comes up, not in a minute. Three to five words is enough: who, what, by when.
3. If it has a date, save it as a task with a due date and a reminder.
4. Look at the list at a set time each day so captured items turn into actions.
Why it helps: new information can push out what you were holding, so the memory fails before you can act on it. Writing it down moves the job of remembering out of your head.
Try saying: If it matters, it goes in the note now.
If it does not work: use a voice memo if typing is too slow.
title: Write it down the moment you hear it

source_document: Marla Cummins: How This Weekly Habit Helps ADHD Adults Follow Through (updated Sep 29, 2026); Unattributed AI-generated search overview on ADHD calendars and reminders (user-collected)
source_citation: Practitioner source (coach blog) plus an unattributed AI-generated overview that cites commercial and social media pages. No studies cited for the tip. Use for ideas only.
text:
Recognize it when: appointments and deadlines are scattered across notes, memory and different apps, or your calendar is full of tasks you never do.
Technique: use the calendar only for things with a fixed date and time, and one task list for everything else.
How: 1. Put appointments, classes and deadlines with a set date on the calendar, so they are not left to memory.
2. Put things without a set time on one task list.
3. Leave 15 to 30 minutes between events for travel and for things that run over.
4. Once a week, look ahead far enough to start preparing for what is coming.
Why it helps: a calendar that shows only real commitments can be trusted, and gaps between events protect you from underestimating how long things take.
Try saying: Fixed time goes in the calendar. Everything else goes on the list.
If it does not work: start with just the next two weeks of fixed events.
title: Calendar for fixed commitments, task list for everything else

source_document: Inflow: 8 ways to budget and pay bills on time with ADHD (Ash Fisher, Nov 22, 2021); MossyMind: Out of sight, out of mind with ADHD (Oct 15, 2026); Unattributed AI-generated search overview on ADHD calendars and reminders (user-collected)
source_citation: Practitioner sources, no ADHD trials of this tip. MossyMind cites Gilbert (2015) and Gilbert et al. (2023) on external reminders in general-population samples; verify before quoting. The AI overview is low quality and was used only where the other two agree.
text:
Recognize it when: you set one reminder and it gets dismissed or ignored, or you are too busy to act when it goes off.
Technique: use two or three reminders at different times, and label them with the action.
How: 1. Set a heads-up alert well ahead: 1 to 2 hours before an event, or about a week and two days before a bill or deadline.
2. Set an action alert 15 to 30 minutes before, when you need to start moving.
3. Write the action in the label (Leave for dentist, Pay phone bill), not just the event name.
4. Add one cue you can see, such as a note by the door or a watch buzz.
Why it helps: a single alert is easy to dismiss. Small studies in the general population suggest external reminders improve follow-through, so you do not need to save them for when you are already struggling.
Try saying: One alert is a suggestion. Two or three is a plan.
If it does not work: add one more reminder in a different place, such as a phone alarm plus a note.
title: Set two or three reminders, not one

source_document: AuDHD Psychiatry: Habit Stacking for ADHD (Jun 9, 2025); Marla Cummins: How This Weekly Habit Helps ADHD Adults Follow Through (updated Sep 29, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner sources, no studies cited for the tip. The AuDHD Psychiatry page is a clinic's marketing blog (reviewed by a chartered psychologist). Habit stacking is also covered in the earlier habit-stacking chunk.
text:
Recognize it when: you have a planner or calendar but forget to open it, or you keep starting and stopping a planning routine.
Technique: attach a two-minute planner check to something you already do every day.
How: 1. Pick one daily anchor, such as making coffee, waiting for the kettle, or changing into pyjamas.
2. Decide the tiny action: open the calendar and read today and tomorrow, or write your top three priorities.
3. Put a visual cue where the anchor happens (the planner by the kettle, a sticky note on the mirror).
4. Tick it off on a tracker as a small reward.
5. If you miss days, simplify it and add a cue instead of starting over.
Why it helps: the anchor supplies the reminder, so you rely less on memory or willpower.
Try saying: After I make coffee, I check my calendar.
If it does not work: shrink the action to just opening the calendar, or move it to a different anchor.
title: Forget to check your planner? Attach it to something you already do

source_document: MossyMind: Out of sight, out of mind with ADHD (Oct 15, 2026); Karidi, Remembering the Future, Attention Magazine (CHADD, Dec 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner sources. MossyMind (an app company's blog) cites small studies: Altgassen et al. 2014 (25 adults with ADHD vs 25 controls) and 2019 (29 vs 24). Karidi's tips are the author's suggestions, not trial results. Treat the studies as clues, not settled facts.
text:
Recognize it when: you plan to do something at a set time (call at 3, take the form tomorrow) and the time passes without you remembering, or your usual alarm gets swiped away.
Technique: turn a time-based intention into a cue that shows up on its own, and make that cue distinct, personal and in more than one place.
How: 1. Instead of 'take the form to the pharmacy tomorrow', put the form on top of your keys tonight.
2. Instead of 'call the school at 2', set a phone alarm labelled with the action.
3. Put the item or alarm where you will meet it at the right moment, such as the doormat or front door.
4. Make it stand out: a special alarm tone, a bright sticky note, an object in your shoe. Make it personal, such as a song that reminds you of the person you need to call.
5. Use two places: a phone reminder plus a physical note, or a location reminder that buzzes near the pharmacy.
6. When the cue appears, do the action, or move it to a new time on purpose.
Why it helps: small studies suggest adults with ADHD manage cue-triggered reminders better than remembering at a set time with no cue (groups of about 25 to 30 people). A plain alarm turns into background noise, but an unusual, personal cue in two places is harder to ignore.
Try saying: I will not remember at 3. I will set something that finds me at 3.
If it does not work: change the cue every few weeks, because even strong cues get ignored over time.
title: Turn 'remember at 3 pm' into a cue you cannot miss

source_document: MossyMind: Out of sight, out of mind with ADHD (Oct 15, 2026); Simply Psychology: ADHD and Working Memory (Apr 4, 2026); Karidi, Remembering the Future, Attention Magazine (CHADD, Dec 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner sources citing small studies and meta-analyses second-hand (for example a meta-analysis of 38 studies on working memory, and prospective memory studies with about 25 to 30 people per group). Not verified here. The Simply Psychology page is labelled an AI-assisted draft. Reframing language advice is Karidi's (CHADD, Dec 2025), not trial-tested.
text:
Recognize it when: you tell yourself 'I'll remember' and then do not, or after forgetting you call yourself careless or say 'I just have a terrible memory'.
Technique: treat forgetting as a memory-timing problem: swap 'I'll remember' for a cue or note, and swap harsh labels for words that point to a fix.
How: 1. Notice the trap thought: I'll remember.
2. Ask what will bring this to mind at the right moment. If the answer is nothing, set something up.
3. Write it down, set an alarm, or put the item where you will see it. Do this before the next task, because an interruption can wipe out what you were holding.
4. Catch the harsh sentence and replace it: 'I need a stronger cue' or 'retrieval is where I struggle'.
5. To others, say 'I need reminders to follow through' rather than 'I'm so forgetful'.
Why it helps: remembering to do something later means holding an intention while other things compete for attention. Research suggests this is harder on average for adults with ADHD, and it does not mean you do not care. Harsh labels add shame and give you no fix.
Try saying: I am not careless. My memory needs a cue.
If it does not work: if forgetting is causing serious problems at work, with money or with health, talk to a clinician. Memory problems that are new, sudden or getting worse need prompt medical attention. If shame is heavy and constant, a therapist or coach can help.
title: The 'I'll remember' trap: forgetting is not carelessness

source_document: MossyMind: Out of sight, out of mind with ADHD (Oct 15, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source (an app company's blog). The source says there is no trial of storage bins for ADHD, so treat these as experiments. Overlaps in part with the zones-and-homes chunk.
text:
Recognize it when: you put away things you need to act on (a library book, a bill, food) and forget them until it is too late.
Technique: put each item where the action happens, so the item itself reminds you.
How: 1. Put things that must leave the house on a spot by the door or on the doormat.
2. Keep bills and forms that need action in a clear tray, separate from mail you can recycle.
3. Put food that needs eating soon at eye level in the fridge.
4. Keep keys, wallet and charger in one bowl.
5. Keep the visible set small, so a pile of displayed things does not fade into the background.
Why it helps: a visible item prompts you at the right moment, so you depend less on remembering.
Try saying: If I need to act on it, it goes where I will see it.
If it does not work: try it with one item for a week and keep what works.
title: Put things where the action happens so they remind you

source_document: MossyMind: Out of sight, out of mind with ADHD (Oct 15, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source (an app company's blog that sells a task app). No studies cited for this tip. Use the method, not the product.
text:
Recognize it when: tasks are spread across notes, apps and sticky notes, or yesterday's unfinished tasks scroll out of sight and get forgotten.
Technique: keep one daily list you open every day, where unfinished tasks come back to you.
How: 1. Choose one place for today's tasks and make sure everything you must act on shows up there.
2. Keep today short enough to read at a glance, about 3 to 5 tasks.
3. Let unfinished tasks carry forward to today instead of staying on a past date.
4. If a task has rolled over several days, decide: make it smaller, give it a firm date, park it, or delete it.
Why it helps: each extra place is one more thing to remember to check. A task should only leave your sight by being done, rescheduled on purpose, or deleted on purpose.
Try saying: One list, and nothing disappears unless I decide.
If it does not work: shrink today's list to three tasks.
title: One daily list where unfinished tasks come back to you

source_document: Marla Cummins: How This Weekly Habit Helps ADHD Adults Follow Through (updated Sep 29, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source (an ADHD coach's blog with a newsletter sign-up; draws on David Allen's Getting Things Done). No studies cited. The coach suggests trying it imperfectly for at least 8 weeks.
text:
Recognize it when: tasks and commitments keep slipping, you feel busy but not on top of things, or you are driven by whatever is loudest or latest.
Technique: a short weekly review of your inbox, task list, calendar and plan.
How: 1. Pick a set day and place, such as Thursday or Friday morning, so you go into the weekend ready.
2. Process: sort the week's loose papers, notes and missed messages into tasks, files or the bin.
3. Tasks: add new ones, tick off finished ones, and make sure each project has a next action.
4. Calendar: look at upcoming dates and add any preparation tasks.
5. Plan: choose where your time goes next week.
6. Reflect: what went well, and what is getting in the way?
7. Do not do the tasks during the review. Just collect and plan.
Why it helps: it replaces holding everything in your head with a regular check, and it builds confidence that you are not missing something.
Try saying: This is time to plan, not time to do.
If it does not work: do only part of it, and try it imperfectly for several weeks before you judge it.
title: A weekly review so nothing slips through

source_document: Marla Cummins: How This Weekly Habit Helps ADHD Adults Follow Through (updated Sep 29, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source (an ADHD coach's blog). No studies cited. The 'waiting for' list is from David Allen's Getting Things Done, as described by the coach.
text:
Recognize it when: you forgot to reply, you are waiting on someone and never followed up, or a message got buried.
Technique: reply at once if it takes two minutes or less, otherwise capture it, and track what you are waiting for with a follow-up date.
How: 1. If a reply takes two minutes or less, send it now.
2. Otherwise write it down as a task with a due date.
3. When you are waiting on someone, add a task such as 'text Sam if I have not heard back', dated a few days later.
4. Once a week, go through messages from the past week (email, texts, voicemail, chat apps).
5. Treat messages older than a week as a separate catch-up job.
Why it helps: 'waiting for' items are often overlooked because nothing reminds you of them. A dated task does the reminding.
Try saying: If I am waiting, I set a follow-up date.
If it does not work: if quick replies keep turning into long ones, write them down and answer in one set slot.
title: Forgot to reply or follow up: track what you are waiting for

source_document: Inflow: 8 ways to budget and pay bills on time with ADHD (Ash Fisher, Nov 22, 2021)
source_citation: Practitioner source: a company blog based on the writer's own experience, published 2021. No studies cited. Auto-pay can overdraw an account if funds are short.
text:
Recognize it when: you miss bill due dates and pay late fees, or paying bills feels like a monthly emergency.
Technique: set the system up once, so paying bills needs little memory.
How: 1. List every bill with its due date.
2. Put each on a calendar as a monthly repeat, with reminders such as a week and two days before.
3. Use auto-pay for fixed bills if your income is steady, and check you will have enough money in the account that day, to avoid overdraft.
4. Or pay all bills in one sitting on a set day, such as payday, covering the next pay period.
5. Tick bills off on a simple checklist or spreadsheet so you can see what is still outstanding.
6. If it is an option, ask a partner to take over some payments.
Why it helps: it replaces remembering each due date with a one-time setup, and ticking bills off gives a clear picture.
Try saying: Future me will thank me for setting this up once.
If it does not work: start with the one bill you miss most often.
title: Pay bills on time: set it up once

source_document: Karidi, D. Remembering the Future: How ADHD Affects Prospective Memory. Attention Magazine (CHADD), Dec 2025
source_citation: Practitioner article by an ADHD coach and memory researcher in CHADD's magazine, with a reading list but no inline citations. The five-stage description is an explanation, not a tested tool.
text:
Recognize it when: you keep forgetting things you meant to do and feel it is just a bad memory.
Technique: work out where in the chain the plan broke, then fix that one stage.
How: 1. Encoding: did you actually store the plan, or did something interrupt you as you heard it? Fix: write it down at once.
2. Holding it: did it fade while you were busy? Fix: put it somewhere you will see it later.
3. Noticing the cue: did the moment come and you did not notice? Fix: make the cue louder or tie it to an event.
4. Doing it: did you remember but not act? Fix: shrink the first step to something tiny.
5. Checking: did you do it but wonder later? Fix: tick it off somewhere right after.
Why it helps: remembering the future takes five steps, so a slip at any one looks like forgetting. Naming the stage points to a fix and replaces blame with problem-solving.
Try saying: Which step failed this time: storing it, holding it, noticing the cue, doing it, or checking it?
If it does not work: if the same stage fails every time, ask a coach or clinician for help designing a support for it.
title: When you forget something, find which stage failed

source_document: Karidi, D. Remembering the Future: How ADHD Affects Prospective Memory. Attention Magazine (CHADD), Dec 2025
source_citation: Practitioner article in CHADD's magazine. Described as support the author uses with clients, not as a tested treatment.
text:
Recognize it when: you plan to do something but keep not starting, or you stay on track only when someone is around.
Technique: work alongside another person, or let someone know your plan so they can nudge you.
How: 1. Pick the task and a time. Ask someone to be present in person or on a video call while you work on your own task.
2. Or make the plan visible: tell a friend 'I will walk at 6' and ask them to text 'ready for our walk?'.
3. Keep it light. The other person does not have to do anything but be there or check in.
4. A coach or therapist can also give structure for planning and tracking progress.
Why it helps: another person's presence adds gentle pressure and cuts distraction, and a check-in works as a reminder from outside your head.
Try saying: Can you sit with me for 20 minutes while I do this?
If it does not work: if you feel judged, choose someone who is calm and not invested in the result, or use a virtual coworking room.
title: Body doubling and a text from a friend can carry follow-through

source_document: Inflow: Texting with ADHD, 6 ways to stop ghosting your friends (Quentin Görres, Oct 27, 2022)
source_citation: Practitioner source: a company blog post by a freelance writer with ADHD, drawing on his own experience. It cites one study on messages opened at a bad time (not verified here).
text:
Recognize it when: you are sure you replied, but the other person is still waiting, or you answered in your head and never sent it.
Technique: look at the thread and set a daily reminder to check whether the important ones were really sent.
How: 1. Open the message thread and check that your reply is there, not just in your head.
2. Set a daily reminder to scan messages from the people who matter most.
3. If you cannot answer now, leave the message unopened until you can, so it does not look dealt with.
4. Reply right away if you already know what to say.
Why it helps: opening a message at a bad moment makes the alert disappear, and a reply written only in your head feels done. A set check catches both.
Try saying: I will check the thread, not trust that I replied.
If it does not work: if you often leave replies half-written, send a short one now and add detail later.
title: Did you actually reply? Check, because you may have only answered in your head

source_document: Inflow: Texting with ADHD, 6 ways to stop ghosting your friends (Quentin Görres, Oct 27, 2022)
source_citation: Practitioner source: a company blog post by a freelance writer with ADHD. Strategies are suggestions from experience.
text:
Recognize it when: messages pile up, you feel overwhelmed by the buzzing, or you avoid your phone because of it.
Technique: reply in a scheduled slot and keep only the alerts that matter.
How: 1. Pick a daily slot to read and answer messages together.
2. Keep a sticky note by your workspace listing who you need to text before the end of the day.
3. Turn off notification permissions for non-essential apps, so texts and email are not buried.
4. If a long reply feels heavy, send a quick voice message or make a call instead.
Why it helps: an inbox that buzzes all day causes overwhelm, and giving up on all of it is a common response. A fixed slot plus fewer alerts makes the job smaller.
Try saying: I answer messages at 5, and only the important apps get to buzz.
If it does not work: if the slot gets skipped, attach it to an existing routine such as after dinner.
title: Set a time to reply to messages and cut the alerts that bury them

source_document: Inflow: Texting with ADHD, 6 ways to stop ghosting your friends (Quentin Görres, Oct 27, 2022)
source_citation: Practitioner source: a company blog post by a freelance writer with ADHD. The 'shame cycle' claim cites a source not verified here.
text:
Recognize it when: you have not replied to a friend for days, and the longer it gets the harder it feels to answer.
Technique: break the shame cycle with a short, imperfect reply.
How: 1. Remind yourself it is probably a text, and the other person is not holding their breath.
2. Write one or two lines. A simple 'sorry for the slow reply, how are you?' is enough.
3. Skip the long explanation and the perfect GIF.
4. Send it before you start the next task.
Why it helps: avoidance, then anxiety, then guilt and shame can feed more avoidance. A short reply stops the loop and is usually received better than silence.
Try saying: Late and short beats perfect and never.
If it does not work: if you cannot face typing, use a voice message or a quick call.
title: Replied far too late? Send a short reply instead of avoiding it

source_document: ADHD Planner blog: I Missed a Deadline at Work Because of ADHD. Now What? (Ravi Mishra)
source_citation: Practitioner source: an ADHD planner app's blog by a writer who says it is personal experience, not medical advice. It cites a 2026 systematic review linking ADHD symptoms and procrastination, with mostly cross-sectional studies. The page promotes its own app; the method does not depend on it.
text:
Recognize it when: a deadline is slipping or has passed and you want to hide until it is done.
Technique: tell your manager early with a new date you can meet and what they will get first.
How: 1. Message them before they have to ask, so they can adjust their own plans.
2. Use three parts: what is late, what they get and when, and a short apology. For example: 'The report due today isn't ready. You'll have the summary section by 3 and the full draft tomorrow at noon. Sorry for the slip.'
3. Pick a new date you are confident you can beat.
4. Then list what is left in pieces small enough to finish in one sitting, with rough times. Double the time on anything new.
5. Close everything that is not this task, including your inbox, and do the piece you promised first.
Why it helps: early notice lets others adapt, and shrinking the work from one wall to pieces makes starting possible.
Try saying: It's late. Here is what you get and when. Sorry for the slip.
If it does not work: you do not have to say why. If misses keep happening, ask about accommodations, which is when a medical reason becomes relevant.
title: Missed a deadline: tell your manager within the hour

source_document: ADHD Planner blog: I Missed a Deadline at Work Because of ADHD. Now What? (Ravi Mishra)
source_citation: Practitioner source: an ADHD planner app's blog, personal experience not medical advice. The three causes are the author's categories.
text:
Recognize it when: you finished the late work and want to stop it happening again.
Technique: ask which of three things went wrong, and fix only that one.
How: 1. Started too late: the work would have fit but began the day before. Make your own earlier deadlines inside the project.
2. Bigger than it looked: the estimate was off. Break the project into steps on day one and time the first two.
3. The date fell out of view: you knew, then it was nowhere you looked. Set a reminder a few days ahead, attached to the first step as well as the due date.
4. Write down which one it was, so patterns show over time.
Why it helps: each cause needs a different fix, and checking it once is quicker than guessing. One miss is a bad week; a pattern is worth a conversation.
Try saying: Which was it: late start, bigger than it looked, or lost date?
If it does not work: if it keeps happening, talk to your manager about accommodations such as written instructions, task lists and reminders.
title: After a missed deadline, find where it slipped

source_document: Assignment Help Center: Deadline Extensions for ADHD & Dyslexia (Jun 22, 2026)
source_citation: LOW-TRUST source. The page is on a site that sells essay-writing services, so it has a commercial interest. Its order-data statistics were NOT used. Only the general idea (a documented, recurring accommodation via a university disability office) was used. Rules vary by country and institution, so check the university's own policy.
text:
Recognize it when: you ask tutors for a few extra days again and again and dread re-explaining yourself.
Technique: register with the disability or student support service early so an adjustment is documented once.
How: 1. Contact the disability or accessibility service at the start of a term, not the night before a deadline.
2. Bring evidence if you have it, such as a diagnosis or letter from a clinician. If you have none yet, ask what interim support is possible.
3. Describe the real impact, for example 'planning and sequencing take me far longer', not just 'I struggle'.
4. Ask for the agreed adjustment to be written into your support plan and confirmed in writing, and review it each year.
5. Use extra time on planning: break each task into stages.
Why it helps: a documented plan means you do not re-justify yourself under stress. It changes your timeline, not the standard the work is marked against.
Try saying: I would like an ongoing adjustment, recorded in my plan.
If it does not work: if it is delayed or refused, ask for the reason in writing, escalate within the service, and keep records. Do not pay anyone to write your work.
title: Ask once for a standing adjustment instead of begging for each extension

source_document: CBT Los Angeles: Part 4, CBT and Mood (excerpt from Leahy, Holland & McGinn, Treatment Plans and Interventions for Depression and Anxiety Disorders, 2nd ed., Guilford, 2011)
source_citation: Textbook excerpt (Leahy, Holland & McGinn, 2011, Guilford Press), published on a therapy practice's site. General CBT teaching, not ADHD-specific.
text:
Recognize it when: you say 'I feel like I did a bad job' or 'I feel like you are not listening', and the feeling stays unclear.
Technique: split the thought from the emotion.
How: 1. Write the sentence you said, such as 'I feel like I did a bad job'.
2. Ask: is this a thought about something, or a feeling? 'I did a bad job' is a thought.
3. Find the feeling underneath, in one word: ashamed, worried, disappointed.
4. Write both: Thought: I did a bad job. Feeling: ashamed.
Why it helps: thoughts and feelings get mixed up in everyday speech. Separating them shows what you are reacting to and which one to work on.
Try saying: Is that a thought or a feeling? What is the one-word feeling?
If it does not work: it is fine to find this tricky at first. Start with just one example a day.
title: 'I feel like...' is often a thought, not a feeling

source_document: CBT Los Angeles: Part 4, CBT and Mood (excerpt from Leahy, Holland & McGinn, Treatment Plans and Interventions for Depression and Anxiety Disorders, 2nd ed., Guilford, 2011)
source_citation: Textbook excerpt (Leahy, Holland & McGinn, 2011), shown on a therapy practice's site. The sample is a general CBT worksheet, not ADHD-specific.
text:
Recognize it when: your mood swings feel random and you cannot see what sets them off.
Technique: track your emotions for one week with four short steps.
How: 1. Write a brief factual description of the situation, such as 'argument with my spouse'.
2. Write the emotion or emotions you felt.
3. Rate each at its peak from 1 (mild) to 10 (extreme).
4. Note body signs: heartbeat, breathing, tension, heaviness, shaking, heat or cold.
5. Fill it in at the same time each day, such as after dinner, and set a phone alarm or keep it on your nightstand.
Why it helps: tracking builds emotional awareness and shows patterns over time. Body signals can tell you a feeling is there when you cannot name it.
Try saying: Situation, feeling, how strong, what my body did.
If it does not work: if you miss a day, skip it and carry on, since a few entries still show patterns.
title: A one-week mood log: situation, feeling, intensity, body

source_document: DBT-Mind: Emotion Regulation Skills (Timo, updated Oct 29, 2026); Kind Mind Psychology: The PLEASE Skill in DBT (Wenzhen Li, Mar 26, 2026); Medical News Today: What could cause rapid mood swings? (Villines, medically reviewed, Apr 14, 2021)
source_citation: Three sources: an app company's guide, a therapy practice's blog that advertises its services, and a medically reviewed health article. General DBT and health teaching, not ADHD trials. Consult a clinician for medical conditions.
text:
Recognize it when: your emotions have been unusually raw, your mood flips quickly, or the same trigger hits harder than usual.
Technique: audit the PLEASE areas and other physical causes before trying any other technique.
How: 1. Physical illness: treat it and keep appointments. Hormonal changes and illness can also affect mood.
2. Eating: do not skip meals, since low blood sugar makes small things feel huge.
3. Alcohol, drugs and medication: notice whether mood changes after a new medicine, alcohol or drugs, and ask your prescriber. Do not change medication on your own.
4. Sleep: keep a regular routine, limit screens before bed, and keep the room cool and dark. Tiredness makes small things feel huge.
5. Exercise: choose something you enjoy, such as a walk.
6. Pick one area and make a small change, not all of them. Write down what happened before a swing to spot a pattern.
Why it helps: the same trigger can land very differently after eight hours of sleep than after four. Many mood swings have treatable causes, so treat them as a health matter, not a personal failure.
Try saying: Before I judge my mood, have I slept, eaten and taken my medication?
If it does not work: if you feel exhausted no matter how much you sleep, or the swings are severe, see a doctor. If sleep is the problem despite good habits, talk to a clinician, because ADHD and sleep trouble often go together.
title: Raw emotions or mood swings? Check sleep, food, health, medication and movement first

source_document: Unattributed AI-generated search overview on DBT TIPP, 5-4-3-2-1 and self-soothing (user-collected)
source_citation: LOW-TRUST source: an unattributed AI-generated overview with links to a clinic blog, a meditation app and YouTube. The technique is widely taught, but this source is weak, so confirm with a clinical source.
text:
Recognize it when: anxious thoughts are racing, or you are caught in rumination.
Technique: anchor your attention in what you can sense now.
How: 1. Name 5 things you can see.
2. Name 4 things you can touch or feel, such as your feet on the floor.
3. Name 3 sounds you can hear.
4. Name 2 things you can smell.
5. Name 1 thing you can taste.
6. Go slowly, and say or count them out loud if it helps.
Why it helps: pulling attention to the senses can interrupt an anxious loop and bring you back to the present.
Try saying: Five things I can see right now are...
If it does not work: if it feels like too much, stop at the sight and touch steps, or do not use it if it raises distress and speak to a clinician.
title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding when your mind is racing

source_document: Unattributed AI-generated search overview on DBT TIPP, 5-4-3-2-1 and self-soothing (user-collected); Neurodivergent Insights (Dr Megan Anna Neff): Sensory Calming Techniques (updated Oct 2026)
source_citation: LOW-TRUST: an unattributed AI-generated overview of DBT TIPP, with a note from Neurodivergent Insights that breathing strategies do not work for everyone. Cold-water and intense exercise steps carry safety limits, so confirm with a clinician.
text:
Recognize it when: your distress is very high (about 6 or more out of 10) and thinking will not help.
Technique: change your body state first, using one safe step.
How: 1. Cool: splash cool water on your face for 15 to 30 seconds. Skip this if you have a heart condition, an eating disorder, or a medical reason not to, and ask your clinician.
2. Move: a brisk walk or a few minutes of jumping jacks, if it is safe for you.
3. Breathe: breathe out longer than in, for example in for 4 and out for 6.
4. Tense and release: tighten shoulders or fists for 5 seconds, then let go.
5. Do one step, then rate the feeling again.
Why it helps: these steps change body arousal, which can lower intensity before you work on thoughts. If breath cues are hard to feel, breathing may not help, so try another step.
Try saying: I will change my body first, then think.
If it does not work: if distress stays extreme or you feel unsafe, contact a clinician or your local emergency number or crisis line.
title: Body-first calm-down for peak distress: cool, move, breathe

source_document: Unattributed AI-generated search overview on DBT TIPP, 5-4-3-2-1 and self-soothing (user-collected); Neurodivergent Insights (Dr Megan Anna Neff): Sensory Calming Techniques (updated Oct 2026)
source_citation: Low-to-moderate trust: an unattributed AI-generated overview plus a clinical psychologist's blog. Preferences differ widely.
text:
Recognize it when: you are upset and fighting the feeling is making it worse.
Technique: give yourself comfort through one or more senses.
How: 1. Sight: look at a calming photo or nature scene.
2. Sound: calming music, nature sounds, brown noise or a friend's voice.
3. Smell: lavender, coffee, vanilla or fresh air.
4. Taste: warm herbal tea or a favourite treat.
5. Touch: a weighted or soft blanket, a warm mug, a pet or a warm shower.
Why it helps: gentle comfort helps you ride out distress without making it worse. What soothes one person can grate on another.
Try saying: What is one comfort I can give myself right now?
If it does not work: if a sense irritates you, drop it and keep the others.
title: Self-soothe with the five senses

source_document: ADDA: ADHD & Sensory Overload (ADDA Editorial Team, Apr 6, 2023)
source_citation: Association article (ADDA editorial team, 2023) with academic references (for example Bijlenga et al., 2017; Lane & Reynolds, 2019). Sensory processing differences are common in ADHD but not part of diagnostic criteria.
text:
Recognize it when: lights, noise, smells, crowds or textures make you irritable, anxious, restless or unable to focus.
Technique: find what overwhelms you and reduce it.
How: 1. Notice where and when you get overwhelmed, and jot down the triggers: sounds, lights, smells, crowds, fabrics, doing too many things at once.
2. Reduce exposure: adjustable lights, scent-free products, comfortable clothes, avoiding peak hours.
3. Use aids: noise-cancelling headphones, earplugs, sunglasses, a weighted blanket.
4. Plan to leave events earlier, or suggest a quieter place.
5. After an episode, find a quiet space, breathe, and recover.
Why it helps: your reaction is real, not just in your head. Cutting exposure lowers how much your system has to handle.
Try saying: That noise is too much for me. Can we go somewhere quieter?
If it does not work: if overload is frequent, an occupational therapist can help design routines and changes.
title: Sensory overload: spot your triggers and cut exposure

source_document: Neurodivergent Insights (Dr Megan Anna Neff): Sensory Calming Techniques (updated Oct 2026)
source_citation: Psychologist's blog (Neurodivergent Insights) with affiliate links, so product suggestions were left out. Written from clinical and lived experience. The author notes what helps varies by person and by day.
text:
Recognize it when: overload has already started and you cannot think of what helps.
Technique: keep two or three soothers ready.
How: 1. Before it happens, tick what already works: less input, deep pressure, movement, rhythm, temperature, sound, scent, something for the hands, time outdoors.
2. Pick two or three and keep them close, such as headphones and a playlist.
3. When overload hits, start with less input, then add one soother.
4. Re-check the list now and then, because what helps can change.
Why it helps: soothers help once overload has begun, and having a list ready saves you from thinking of ideas when you are depleted.
Try saying: My soothers are... I will pick one now.
If it does not work: if nothing helps, rest in a quiet dark space and consider talking to a clinician.
title: Build a short list of sensory soothers for overload

source_document: WebMD: Bipolar Disorder or ADHD? (Madeline Laguaite, medically reviewed by Smitha Bhandari MD, Aug 21, 2024); Medical News Today: What could cause rapid mood swings? (Zawn Villines, medically reviewed by Kendra Kubala PsyD, Apr 14, 2021)
source_citation: Two medically reviewed articles. The WebMD article is about children and teens, with overlap noted for adults. This chunk is NOT a diagnosis tool. It exists to prompt a professional check.
text:
Recognize it when: your mood swings are intense, long-lasting or come in episodes, or you notice very little sleep with lots of energy, or low mood that will not lift.
Technique: know the signs that deserve a professional check, and do not self-diagnose.
How: 1. ADHD problems are usually ongoing: inattention, restlessness, impulsivity. Bipolar disorder is a mood disorder that tends to come in episodes with periods of typical mood between.
2. Signs of a manic episode include needing little sleep without tiring, racing talk and thoughts, feeling invincible, and risky behaviour.
3. Signs of depression include a low or irritable mood that does not go away, losing interest, big changes in appetite or sleep, feelings of worthlessness, and thoughts of death or suicide.
4. If symptoms last about a week or more, or worry you, book a clinician. Ask for evaluation over time, not one visit.
5. If you think about suicide or are in danger, contact your local emergency number or crisis line now.
Why it helps: the two can overlap or occur together, and the right treatment differs, so a clinician needs to sort it out.
Try saying: I am not sure what this is, so I will get it checked.
If it does not work: if you are in crisis, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line right away.
title: When mood swings may be more than ADHD: when to get checked

source_document: The ADDvocacy Project (Caroline Beresford): ADHD Overthinking Loops (Feb 28, 2025); Neural Revolution: ADHD & Overthinking, How to Break the Loop
source_citation: Two ADHD coaching businesses' blogs. The neuroscience claims on those pages were not used and were not verified here. The techniques are the coaches' suggestions, not trial results.
text:
Recognize it when: you replay a conversation, analyse a decision, or cannot switch your mind off.
Technique: notice the loop, name it out loud, and observe it without arguing.
How: 1. Pause and ask: what triggered this loop? Is this thought useful, or is my brain just stuck?
2. Name it out loud or in writing: 'I am in an analysis loop about this report'.
3. Observe it without fighting. Suppressing a thought tends to make it louder.
4. Switch to something physical for a few minutes, such as a short walk, paying attention to your feet and breath.
Why it helps: naming a loop gives you a little distance from it, and moving your body interrupts it.
Try saying: I am in a loop. I do not have to follow it.
If it does not work: if loops take over an hour of your day or hurt work or relationships, ask a clinician or coach for help.
title: Stuck in a thought loop: pause, name it, observe it

source_document: The ADDvocacy Project (Caroline Beresford): ADHD Overthinking Loops (Feb 28, 2025)
source_citation: ADHD coach's blog, based on client examples shared with permission. Not tested in trials.
text:
Recognize it when: after a meeting or social event you keep replaying what you said.
Technique: end the event with a short routine that moves your mind on.
How: 1. Do a minute of grounding breathing.
2. Take a quick walk outside.
3. Write down three things you did well in the meeting.
4. Then start the next task straight away.
Why it helps: a fixed routine gives your mind a signal that the event is over and reduces the urge to replay.
Try saying: The event is over. Reset, then next task.
If it does not work: if replaying continues, text a trusted person to check how it went.
title: An after-event reset when you replay meetings or conversations

source_document: The ADDvocacy Project (Caroline Beresford): ADHD Overthinking Loops (Feb 28, 2025)
source_citation: ADHD coach's blog with client examples. The playful names are the author's own approach. Not tested in trials.
text:
Recognize it when: you jump to 'I came across as rude' or 'I messed up again' after a neutral interaction.
Technique: talk back to the critical voice, or ask a trusted person.
How: 1. Give the critical voice a silly name so it feels separate from you.
2. Ask: would I talk to a friend this way? What is a kinder reading of what happened?
3. Ask a trusted person: did I come across okay? Am I overthinking this?
4. Then ask: is this good enough to move forward? Will it matter in a year?
Why it helps: the critic thrives in silence, and outside feedback is often the quickest way to break the loop.
Try saying: Would I say that to a friend?
If it does not work: choose one reality-check person who is kind and honest, not someone who adds worry.
title: Name the inner critic and ask a trusted person for a reality check

source_document: The ADDvocacy Project (Caroline Beresford): ADHD Overthinking Loops (Feb 28, 2025)
source_citation: ADHD coach's blog. Suggestions from the coach, not trial results.
text:
Recognize it when: you lie awake replaying the day or worrying.
Technique: give worries a set time and a place on paper.
How: 1. Choose a daily worry time, earlier than bedtime, for about 10 to 15 minutes.
2. Write worries in a notebook, with one possible next step for each.
3. Keep a notebook by the bed. If a worry arrives at night, write it down and tell yourself it has a slot tomorrow.
4. Wind down with a bedtime ritual or a guided meditation made for ADHD.
Why it helps: writing a worry down lets your mind put it away.
Try saying: I will worry about this at 5 tomorrow. For now it is on paper.
If it does not work: if night worries are constant or you cannot sleep for weeks, see a clinician.
title: Worries at night: schedule worry time and keep a worry journal

source_document: Neural Revolution: ADHD & Overthinking, How to Break the Loop
source_citation: ADHD coaching company's blog. Neuroscience explanations on the page were not used and not verified. The suggestion of movement is the coach's. Another source cited there (Zylowska 2008) was not checked.
text:
Recognize it when: your mind keeps spinning and sitting still makes it worse.
Technique: choose movement that needs your attention.
How: 1. Pick something coordinated: dancing, martial arts, climbing, or a team sport.
2. If you cannot, take a brisk walk and pay deliberate attention to footfall and breath.
3. Do it for at least five minutes.
4. Pair it with a note about what you will do next.
Why it helps: movement that demands attention leaves less room for the loop.
Try saying: I will move for five minutes, then decide.
If it does not work: if you cannot move much, try a short walking meditation naming what you see, hear and feel.
title: Use coordinated movement to break a thought loop

source_document: Neurodivergent Insights (Dr Megan Anna Neff): ADHD Burnout Recovery (updated Oct 2026)
source_citation: Clinical psychologist's blog (Neurodivergent Insights, updated 2026) citing several studies. The author says research on ADHD burnout is thin, there is no clinical definition, and there are no trials of a specific protocol. Not a substitute for care.
text:
Recognize it when: you are exhausted, behind on appointments, messages and forms, and pushing harder makes it worse.
Technique: lower the load instead of adding more.
How: 1. Delegate, simplify, postpone or say no to what you can.
2. Close a few small open loops, such as one email, one bill or one cancelled commitment.
3. Let go of some tasks on purpose instead of carrying a long unspoken list.
4. Reduce sensory load: fewer notifications, less clutter, more time outdoors.
5. Make sleep a priority, and rest in ways that do not feel like demands.
Why it helps: open loops cost working memory and effort. Adding more demanding tasks does not rebuild capacity.
Try saying: I do not have to do everything. Which three things can I drop or shrink?
If it does not work: if it feels like depression, lasts, or you have thoughts of harming yourself, talk to a clinician. If in danger, contact your local emergency number or crisis line.
title: Burnt out: reduce demand and close a few small loops, instead of pushing

source_document: Neurodivergent Insights (Dr Megan Anna Neff): ADHD Burnout Recovery (updated Oct 2026)
source_citation: Clinical psychologist's blog (2026), based on clinical and lived experience. The cycle is described, not tested in a trial.
text:
Recognize it when: you get absorbed for hours, skip meals and sleep, then crash.
Technique: set simple stops while absorbed.
How: 1. Before you start, set a timer or two alarms for food, water, and bedtime.
2. Put a drink and a snack in sight.
3. When the alarm goes off, stand up and stretch before you decide whether to continue.
4. Plan a gentler day after a very intense one.
Why it helps: while absorbed, signals like hunger and tiredness are muted, and the crash comes when they all arrive at once.
Try saying: Alarms protect the thing I enjoy.
If it does not work: if alarms are ignored, ask someone to check in at a set time.
title: Hyperfocus then crash: put bumper rails around it
